newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - Germany in EMU despite economic struggles.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Germany in EMU despite economic struggles.

text.p: Germany faces an uphill battle to whip its economy into shape for European economic and monetary union (EMU), but is nevertheless certain to become a founder member of the single currency club, two Reuters polls showed on Wednesday.

All 49 Europe-wide respondents in a monthly Reuters poll said Germany would be in EMU's first wave, scheduled for January 1999. When asked to put a percentage likelihood on Germany being a founder member, the median forecast from the 49 responses was 100 percent.

But Germany's economic situation is more likely to hinder than help, with the country set to meet just two of the main economic criteria for membership laid down in the Maastricht Treaty, according to a quarterly poll of how economies are shaping up to meet the EMU convergence criteria.
But this is not going to block Europe's economic heavyweight from taking its place on the launch pad of the single currency, analysts said.

"People are thinking that the future of Europe will not be decided by a bunch of accountants. These are aspirations, these are targets," said Dominick Sutton, chief economist at Gandon Capital Markets in Dublin.
"It's great if everybody gets them but the whole future of Europe as they see it will not be determined by one or two numbers which are probably not that accurate," he added.

The median of forecasts from 29 economic analysts across Europe showed Germany narrowly failing to meet the budget deficit-to-gross domestic product (GDP) ratio target of three percent. Its budget deficit is forecast to come in at 3.2 percent, the poll showed, a slight worsening from the 3.05 percent average predicted in the previous poll published in February.

The government's target is 2.9 percent, but sluggish economic growth could put this in jeopardy and many analysts expect it to be revised upwards after tax estimates for 1997 are released on Thursday. Analysts expect a shortfall of around 16 billion marks.

"Due to lower-than-expected growth, tax revenues will fall short of expectations and on the expenditure side, low growth has led to a jump in the unemployment numbers," said Gerlof de Grij, senior bond analyst at ABN AMRO Hoare Govett in Amsterdam.
The total debt-to-GDP ratio, which the average from 27 analysts put at 62 percent, fell just short of the 60 percent target laid down in the treaty.
So the political will behind the project could lead to a tweaking of the criteria to allow Germany in, the experts said.
"There is a lot of political prestige in the whole project. If they dont initiate EMU in 1999, both the political and the economic costs could be significant," said one economist at a Danish bank.

But a worry for Germans is that if they break the rules for themselves, they could open the floodgates to countries like Italy, which is battling hard to meet the Maastricht criteria. They fear the admittance of countries such as Italy could weaken the euro.

"The Germans want to reduce the budget deficit below three percent and the main problem is that if their deficit is a little above, it will be difficult not to exclude Spain and maybe Italy," the Danish economist said.
